worst.subject: character:char_saint_dunstan
worst.why: Saint Dunstan is merely referenced in a hypothetical/legendary comparison by the narrator.

worst.subject: character:char_wise_men
worst.why: The Wise Men are only mentioned in a historical/biblical allusion within a character's dialogue.

worst.subject: character:char_the_parrot
worst.why: The parrot is an imaginary figure from Robinson Crusoe recalled by Scrooge.

worst.subject: location:loc_belle_s_parlour
worst.why: The text only mentions 'a room' without naming or identifying it as a parlour.

worst.subject: relationship:rel_055
worst.why: The text mentions Mrs. Fezziwig and the three Miss Fezziwigs, but does not explicitly define their parent-child relationship.

worst.subject: relationship:rel_092
worst.why: The passage shows Master Peter and Bob in the same household, but does not explicitly state that Bob is his father.

worst.subject: state_update:ev_0358:char_charwoman.location_id
worst.why: The location is Old Joe's parlour, not Belle's parlour.

worst.subject: event:ev_0420
worst.why: The text states he wrote the address, but does not state he wrote it on a parcel (the turkey had not even arrived yet).

events.truth_text: Fred visits, wishes his uncle a merry Christmas, and invites him to dinner; Scrooge answers 'Bah! Humbug!' and refuses
two portly gentlemen ask Scrooge for a subscription for the poor; he asks whether there are no prisons, no workhouses
told that many would rather die than go there, Scrooge answers that they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population
Scrooge grudgingly allows Bob Cratchit the whole of Christmas Day off, calling it a poor excuse for picking a man's pocket every twenty-fifth of December
Scrooge walks home alone through the fog to his gloomy chambers
the door-knocker briefly becomes Marley's face as Scrooge lets himself in
that night, Marley's ghost appears, bound in a chain of cash-boxes, keys, ledgers, and purses
Marley declares he wears the chain he forged in life, link by link and yard by yard, and warns Scrooge his own chain is longer still
Marley shows Scrooge the air outside the window crowded with other chained, wailing phantoms, doomed to see misery they no longer have the power to help
Marley tells Scrooge he will be haunted by Three Spirits, and that this is his one chance and hope
the bell tolls one, and a strange childlike figure — the Ghost of Christmas Past — draws back Scrooge's bed-curtains
the Spirit takes Scrooge by the hand and they pass through the wall together, out into the country of his own boyhood
young Scrooge sits alone in the empty schoolroom at Christmas, forgotten while other boys go home
his sister Fan arrives, radiant, to fetch him home at last, saying their father is much kinder now and the two of them are to be together always
present-day Scrooge is moved almost to tears, and the Spirit reminds him Fan died young, but left a son — Fred
old Fezziwig throws open his warehouse for a joyous Christmas Eve party for his apprentices, young Scrooge among them
the Spirit remarks it is a small thing to be so grateful for; Scrooge, unsettled, defends Fezziwig — the power to make people happy or unhappy costs so little
Scrooge wishes, watching, that he could say a word or two to his own clerk just now
young Scrooge, older now, hears Belle release him from their engagement, telling him another idol — gain — has displaced her
the Spirit shows Belle years afterward, married to another man, in a warm home crowded with cheerful children
Belle's husband mentions passing Scrooge's office that day: a lone light, his partner Marley dying, and Scrooge himself sitting quite alone, as he always is
Scrooge, unable to bear it, seizes the extinguisher-cap and begs the Spirit to remove him and show him no more
Scrooge wakes in his own room, transformed by a mound of Christmas food and greenery, presided over by a jovial giant of a Spirit
the Ghost of Christmas Present takes Scrooge out into the Christmas morning streets
the Cratchits sit down to a small, poor, entirely happy Christmas dinner — one goose, a pudding everyone privately feared and no one says aloud might fail
Tiny Tim, who has been to church and hopes people saw his crutch, since it might do them good to remember who made lame beggars walk and blind men see
Scrooge, anxious for the first time, asks the Spirit if Tiny Tim will live

the Spirit answers that if these shadows remain unaltered by the future, the child will die — then quotes Scrooge's own words back to him: that he had better do it, and decrease the surplus population
Scrooge is overcome with penitence and grief and casts his eyes down, ashamed
the Spirit shows Scrooge a bleak mine, where the miners keep Christmas underground with an old song
a solitary lighthouse, where the keepers grip hands and wish each other merry Christmas over the roar of the sea
a ship at sea, where every man aboard hums a Christmas tune to himself, thinking of those at home
Fred's party plays games, including Yes and No, guessing at 'a most disagreeable animal' that turns out to be Uncle Scrooge himself, to general laughter
Fred toasts his uncle anyway, wishing him a merry Christmas and a happy new year, whatever he thinks of the toast
Scrooge, invisible to the party, is in such a mood that he begs the Spirit to let them stay a little longer, and joins in the games in spirit
the Ghost of Christmas Present visibly ages through the night, and at the last shows Scrooge two wretched, wolfish children hidden in its robes: a boy and a girl
the Spirit names them Ignorance and Want, and warns Scrooge to beware them both, but most of all beware Ignorance
Scrooge asks if they have no refuge; the Spirit throws his own words back at him once more — are there no prisons, no workhouses
the bell strikes twelve; the Ghost of Christmas Present vanishes, and a solemn, hooded phantom approaches
the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come, silent and shrouded, leads Scrooge among businessmen on the Exchange
the men discuss an unnamed man's death with complete indifference — one will only attend the funeral if lunch is provided
Scrooge does not recognize anyone they describe, and does not think to ask whose death it is
a charwoman, a laundress (Mrs. Dilber), and an undertaker's man sell Old Joe the dead man's bed-curtains, shirt off his back, and blankets
Old Joe pays them out, remarking the man frightened everyone away from him alive and so has made them all the richer now he's dead
Scrooge is horrified by the scene but still does not connect it to himself
the Spirit brings Scrooge to a bare, dark room where a covered body lies, plundered and bereft, unwatched, unwept, uncared for
Scrooge, trembling, is invited to lift the covering and see the dead man's face, and cannot bring himself to do it
he asks the Spirit to show him some tenderness connected with a death, anywhere, if only one
Caroline and her husband, deep in debt to the dead man, learn of his death
their first feeling is relief: whoever inherits the debt may show them mercy the dead man never would
Scrooge understands, without being told, that no one anywhere has shed one genuine tear for this man
the Cratchit household is quiet and subdued; Tiny Tim has died
Tiny Tim's little crutch is kept, without its owner, in a corner
Bob Cratchit returns from arranging a burial-place, breaks down, then composes himself for the other children's sake
Bob recalls how gentle and patient Tim always was, and says he will never forget it, nor his first words after the day he died
the Spirit brings Scrooge to a neglected, grass-choked grave and points down at the stone
Scrooge begs to know first whether these are the shadows of things that Will be, or only of things that May be
he reads the name on the stone: EBENEZER SCROOGE
he clutches at the Spirit's robe and swears he is not the man he was, and will honor Christmas in his heart and try to keep it all the year
he vows to sponge out the writing on the stone, if it is still possible
Scrooge wakes in his own bed, in his own room, and finds it is still Christmas morning — he has all three Spirits' time to do good in
he laughs, cries, and talks to himself in delight, hardly able to believe it

he leans out the window and asks a boy in his Sunday clothes what day it is, then sends him to buy the prize turkey hanging in the poulterer's, twice the size of Tiny Tim, and have it sent to Bob Cratchit's, anonymously
he dresses in his best and goes out into the street, unable to stop smiling at everyone he passes
Scrooge meets the portly gentleman who solicited him in scene 1, apologizes, and whispers a subscription sum large enough to make the gentleman gasp
Scrooge goes to church, then walks the streets, patting children's heads and delighting in everything he sees
he arrives, trembling, at Fred's door, and asks if he may come in to dinner
Fred welcomes him with open arms, and the party is a wonderful one
Bob Cratchit arrives eighteen and a half minutes late; Scrooge growls in mock severity that this will not do, and that he is about to raise his salary
Bob, terrified for a moment, is then astonished into delight
Scrooge promises to assist Bob's struggling family and to discuss his affairs over a bowl of smoking bishop that very afternoon
the narrator states plainly that Scrooge was better than his word: he did it all, and infinitely more, and to Tiny Tim, who did not die, he was a second father

the narrator closes: Scrooge became as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man as the good old city knew; and it was always said of him that he knew how to keep Christmas well, if any man alive possessed the knowledge
